question: A 16-year-old presents with a six-month history of foul-smelling, scanty ear discharge and progressive hearing loss. On otoscopy you see a posterosuperior pars flaccida marginal perforation with whitish debris. Which combination of features most strongly supports a diagnosis of atticoantral (unsafe) CSOM over tubotympanic (safe) CSOM?

answers.text: Central perforation, profuse mucopurulent discharge, and conductive hearing loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This description fits tubotympanic (safe) CSOM: a central perforation with profuse mucopurulent discharge and no evidence of bone destruction or cholesteatoma. Safe disease is managed medically first.

answers.text: Posterosuperior marginal perforation, foul-smelling scanty discharge, and whitish debris (squamous epithelium)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The triad of posterosuperior/attic marginal perforation, foul-smelling scanty discharge, and whitish flaky debris (keratinous debris of cholesteatoma) is the hallmark of unsafe atticoantral CSOM. This ear requires surgery.

answers.text: Anteroinferior perforation with profuse watery discharge and absent bony erosion on HRCT

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An anteroinferior perforation with watery discharge and no bony erosion on HRCT points to tubotympanic disease, not atticoantral disease. Absence of bony erosion argues strongly against cholesteatoma.

answers.text: Diffuse EAC oedema with thick purulent debris and tragal tenderness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tragal tenderness, EAC oedema, and purulent debris characterise otitis externa (EAC disease), not CSOM (middle ear disease). The tympanic membrane integrity should be assessed to differentiate these conditions.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the classification of CSOM. Unsafe (atticoantral) disease is identified by a posterosuperior or attic marginal perforation, foul-smelling scanty discharge, and the presence of whitish cholesteatoma debris. This pattern demands surgical referral, not prolonged medical treatment.

Well done. Posterosuperior marginal perforation with foul-smelling discharge and whitish keratinous debris is the diagnostic triad of unsafe CSOM — this ear requires mastoid surgery, not topical therapy.
